questions.prompt: What is a release strategy, as distinguished from a deployment plan?
options: The one-time, specific plan for a single release, built from scratch each time
The organization's standing, in-advance decisions about cadence, environment path, and risk tiers, which make writing each individual deployment plan fast and predictable
A Salesforce feature that automatically schedules deployments for you
A document that only applies to Apex code changes, never to declarative changes
A synonym for the Change Advisory Board
A record of every login to a production org
questions.explain: A release strategy is the reusable framework of decisions (cadence, environment path, risk tiers) made once, in advance, so each deployment plan doesn't re-answer the same questions from scratch.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A describes a deployment plan, not a release strategy -- the two are explicitly distinguished in Lesson 1: the strategy is the standing framework, the deployment plan is the one-time application of it to a specific release.

questions.prompt: A release manager wants to schedule a large internal release for the same weekend as Salesforce's Winter seasonal production upgrade. Per Lesson 2, why is this a risky choice?
options: It isn't risky at all -- seasonal upgrades never interact with internal releases

If something breaks afterward, it becomes much harder to tell whether the platform's own seasonal upgrade or the internal release caused the problem, which is why a change-freeze window around the upgrade weekend is standard practice
Salesforce blocks all internal deployments automatically during a seasonal release weekend
Seasonal upgrades only affect sandboxes, so there is no real interaction with a production release
questions.explain: Lesson 2 recommends a change-freeze window around seasonal release weekends specifically so a failure can be cleanly attributed to one cause instead of two overlapping changes.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 1 term to what it actually does.
right: Lays out scheduled internal releases alongside external events like seasonal upgrades
The formal process of requesting, assessing, approving, scheduling, implementing, and verifying a change
Defines how to revert or recover if a specific deployment goes wrong, written before deployment
The standing group that decides whether a specific change is safe to deploy now
questions.explain: Change control is the full request-to-verify lifecycle; the CAB is the standing approval body; a rollback plan is prepared in advance for a specific deployment; and the release calendar coordinates internal releases against external events like seasonal upgrades.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Salesforce ships ________ mandatory seasonal releases per year (Spring, Summer, and Winter), on a schedule the platform sets, not the customer.
questions.explain: Salesforce's three seasonal releases a year -- Spring, Summer, and Winter -- upgrade every org on a schedule Salesforce publishes in advance, not one the customer organization controls.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 4, why can't a change-control policy simply exclude declarative changes (new fields, Flows, validation rules) from review just because they don't go through a code pipeline?
options: Declarative changes can be just as consequential as code changes -- a bad validation rule or Flow can block sales or corrupt data -- so excluding them leaves an ungoverned side door into production
Declarative changes are technically impossible to make in a production org
Only Apex code can ever affect real business processes
Salesforce requires every declarative change to be converted to Apex before deployment
questions.explain: Lesson 4 is explicit that a declarative change can be every bit as risky as a code change, so a policy that only governs code accidentally leaves declarative changes as an invisible, ungoverned path into production.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Change Advisory Boards (CABs), per Lesson 5.
options: A CAB evaluates whether a specific, already-designed change is safe to deploy at a specific time, not whether the underlying idea is architecturally sound
An ECAB is a smaller, faster-acting group empowered to approve emergency changes outside the normal meeting cadence
Emergency changes approved by an ECAB never need to be reviewed again afterward
A CAB that reviews every change with equal depth, regardless of risk, tends to become a bottleneck
A CAB should ideally include perspectives beyond pure technical staff, such as affected business units
questions.explain: A CAB judges deployment safety, not architectural fit (that's the ARB's job). An ECAB speeds up emergency approval but every emergency change still gets a full after-the-fact review -- it is never exempt from review entirely. Reviewing everything with equal depth creates a bottleneck, and mixed CAB membership catches impacts a purely technical review would miss.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of the full change-control lifecycle from Lesson 4 in the correct order.
items: Request -- the change is described, with what it does and why
Assess -- the change is evaluated for risk and impact
Approve -- someone with the authority to decide signs off (or rejects it)
Schedule -- the approved change is placed into a specific release
Implement -- the change is actually deployed
Verify -- the deployment is checked afterward to confirm it worked and didn't break anything else
questions.explain: Change control runs request, assess, approve, schedule, implement, verify -- each stage builds on the previous one, and skipping or reordering them (for example, scheduling before approval) defeats the purpose of the process.

questions.prompt: What is an environment path, as defined in Lesson 7?
options: A single sandbox reused for every single stage of testing and development
The sequence of orgs (sandbox types, then production) a change moves through in order, with each stage designed to catch a different class of problem before it's expensive
The physical network route data takes between two Salesforce data centers
A list of every user who has ever logged into an org
The Salesforce feature that automatically merges two orgs into one
A report showing how many times a Flow has executed
questions.explain: An environment path is the deliberate sequence of stages -- development, integration/QA, UAT, production -- each catching a different class of problem earlier and more cheaply than the next stage would.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A describes exactly the anti-pattern Lesson 7 argues against: using one sandbox for every stage defeats the purpose of a staged environment path, which exists so each stage catches a different kind of problem.

questions.prompt: Match each Salesforce sandbox type to its description from Lesson 7.
right: A complete copy of production data and metadata, refreshing on a longer cycle, suited to final UAT or performance testing
Copies metadata with only a small amount of sample data, refreshing quickly, suited to individual development work
Includes a templated subset of production data plus all metadata, refreshing on a multi-day cycle, suited to QA/UAT
Similar to a Developer sandbox but allows more sample data, suiting slightly larger team or integration testing
questions.explain: Developer sandboxes suit individual work with minimal data; Developer Pro allows more data for team/integration testing; Partial Copy includes a templated, realistic subset of data; Full sandboxes mirror production completely for final validation.

questions.prompt: Two teams each deploy a well-tested automation to the Account object in the same week. After both go live, some records get updated twice with conflicting values, even though neither automation was individually flawed. What does Lesson 8 call this, and what would most directly have helped catch it earlier?
options: A code-quality defect; the fix is better unit testing on each team's automation individually
A metadata conflict; a shared release calendar and cross-team visibility would have surfaced that both teams planned to touch the same object in the same window
A sandbox refresh failure; the fix is refreshing the Full sandbox more often
A licensing issue; the fix is purchasing more Salesforce licenses
questions.explain: This is the textbook metadata-conflict pattern from Lesson 8: two individually sound changes interact badly because nobody coordinated them -- a shared calendar and cross-team visibility is the defense, not more testing of either change in isolation.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about multi-org strategy, per Lesson 8.
options: A single shared org maximizes cross-team data visibility but concentrates coordination problems into one shared environment
Business-unit-specific orgs reduce cross-team metadata conflict but fragment reporting and duplicate administrative overhead
A hub-and-spoke model keeps a central org for shared capabilities with separate business-unit spoke orgs integrated back to it
There is one universally correct org topology that fits every organization regardless of its needs
Unlocked packages eliminate the possibility of any metadata conflict between teams entirely
questions.explain: Lesson 8 explicitly rejects the idea of one universally correct topology -- the right choice depends on the business's actual need for shared data versus independence. Unlocked packages reduce but do not eliminate conflict, since two packages can still touch the same standard object.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in a RACI matrix (Lesson 9), the four letters stand for Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and ________.
questions.explain: RACI stands for Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed -- a way to make role ownership for a release decision explicit rather than assumed.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 10, why should support/help desk staff typically be briefed about a change before end users are?
options: Support staff are legally required to be notified before anyone else under all circumstances
So support isn't blindsided by a change their own users already know about, which would damage credibility for the whole release process
Because support staff always approve changes before the CAB does
Because end users are never informed about changes at all
questions.explain: Lesson 10 explains that being caught off guard by a change end users already know about makes the release process look poorly run -- briefing support ahead of end users avoids that.

questions.prompt: Put these stages of a typical enterprise environment path, from Lesson 7, in the correct order a change moves through on its way to production.
items: Integration/QA sandbox -- multiple developers' work combined and tested together
UAT sandbox -- business users validate the change against real workflows
questions.explain: The environment path runs from individual development through combined integration testing, then business-user UAT, and finally production -- each stage catching a different class of problem before the next, more expensive stage.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 12's Worked Scenario 2, a development team builds a new custom object duplicating an existing one, and the CAB approves the deployment because it's well-built and well-tested. Two months later, reports are inconsistent. What does this scenario demonstrate?
options: That the CAB made an error, since it should have caught the duplication itself
That the CAB correctly judged deployment safety (which is its actual job), but a design-time architecture review board was the missing step that should have caught the duplication before it was built
That duplicate custom objects are always harmless and the inconsistent reports are unrelated
That Salesforce automatically prevents duplicate custom objects from ever being created
questions.explain: The scenario is designed to test whether a reader conflates CAB approval with architectural soundness -- the CAB did its real job correctly; the missing step was an ARB checking for duplication at design time, before any build work started.

questions.prompt: What is technical debt, as defined in Lesson 13?
options: Money an organization owes to Salesforce for extra API calls
The accumulated cost of past shortcuts, unused artifacts, and undocumented decisions that make an org progressively harder and riskier to change over time
A fee charged for using sandboxes beyond their refresh interval
A synonym for Apex code that has failing unit tests
A Salesforce Setup feature that tracks user adoption metrics
The time it takes a seasonal release to reach a specific org instance
questions.explain: Technical debt is the accumulated cost of shortcuts, unused artifacts, and undocumented decisions -- on Salesforce, it shows up heavily in declarative sprawl, not just in code.
questions.distractorExplain: Option A and C invent a financial-fee concept that doesn't exist in this course -- technical debt is a maintainability and risk cost, not a literal monetary charge from Salesforce.

questions.prompt: Match each governance documentation type from Lesson 14 to its description.
right: A short, standard-format record of one significant decision, its alternatives, and the reasoning behind the choice, created once and rarely edited
The strategic-level document defining decision rights, CoE structure, and escalation paths, updated rarely
The actual history of what was deployed, when, and by whom, largely generated as a byproduct of the change-control process
A living record of what each field, object, and major automation is for and who owns it, updated continuously
questions.explain: The charter is the rarely-updated strategic document; the data dictionary is continuously updated; an ADR is created once per significant decision and left as a historical record; release/change records are a byproduct of the change-control process itself.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about architecture review boards (ARBs), per Lesson 15.
options: An ARB operates at design time, before significant build work begins, which is earlier in the lifecycle than the CAB
A proposal that passes ARB review skips the rest of the change-control and CAB process entirely
An ARB reviewing every single proposed field or report would create an even worse bottleneck than an overloaded CAB
A maintained data dictionary helps an ARB check a proposal against existing structure without relying on institutional memory
An ARB is the exact same body as a CAB, just under a different name
questions.explain: An ARB reviews earlier, at design time, and does not replace the later change-control/CAB process -- a proposal that passes ARB review still goes through the full build, test, and CAB process afterward. Reviewing everything would overwhelm the ARB given how early and broadly it would have to operate, and the data dictionary is a direct, practical aid to its review. An ARB and a CAB are explicitly different bodies answering different questions.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 16, a deployment risk is scored along two dimensions -- likelihood and ________.
questions.explain: A deployment risk assessment scores each failure mode on likelihood (how probable) and impact (how severe), which together make risk comparable across different proposed changes.

questions.prompt: A proposed Flow automatically updates a discount field on every Opportunity over $50,000, and three other teams are actively building on the Opportunity object the same month. Per Lesson 16, what should this specific combination of facts do to the risk assessment and the resulting rollback plan?
options: Nothing -- discount automation is always low risk regardless of what else is happening on the same object

It should raise the likelihood score because of metadata-conflict exposure on a shared object, and the rollback plan should specifically address what happens to Opportunity records already touched if the Flow misbehaves, not just a generic 'revert the metadata' statement
It should be ignored, since risk assessments are only required for Apex code, never for Flows
It should automatically cancel all three other teams' work for the month
questions.explain: Per Lesson 16's framework, shared-object activity from other teams raises the likelihood term (metadata-conflict exposure), and because the Flow updates existing records, the rollback plan needs a real, specific answer for already-affected data -- not a generic metadata-only rollback statement.
